paras: The Oconee riot of 1882 was a gun and knife fight at Oconee, Georgia, on Christmas Day, Dec. 25, 1882, in which the town marshal, his son, the mayor and white citizens shot several Black men who resisted an arrest. Three or four Black men were wounded, one of them reported likely to die, and the marshal and his son were also hurt. Georgia and national papers called it a 'riot' and a 'race riot', but their counts of the dead and wounded differed widely.

According to a Sandersville dispatch, several Black men 'under the influence of liquor' became 'very troublesome' at Oconee on Saturday, Dec. 23, and the town marshal, Webster, arrested one of them. The same dispatch said the men returned 'armed' on Monday, which it described as 'very unexpected by the citizens.'

A Toomsboro dispatch said the marshal tried to arrest some Black men who were fighting, was resisted, and that a 'general fight' followed in which Mayor Snell and his sons and the marshal and his son took part. By the Macon account, the five Washington brothers resisted arrest and attacked the marshal, citizens came to his aid, and a man named Ira Lawson joined the brothers, after which 'knives and pistols' were drawn on both sides. The Toomsboro report said the Black men fired first and hit the marshal's son, who then put two bullets into one of them, leaving him 'mortally wounded.'

The Sandersville dispatch counted three Black men shot, one of whom would 'probably die', and said Webster was seriously injured but doing well. The Macon wire printed in New York reported three whites and four Black men wounded, while the St. Paul version named Handy, Jefferson and Squire Washington as 'dangerously wounded.'

On Tuesday, Dec. 26, whites in Oconee heard rumors that Black residents would try to free 'the prisoners' and sent to Toomsboro for help. A marshal from Toomsboro came down with a posse of ten, and the dispatch reported that all was quiet. No report of a death among the wounded Black men, an inquest or a trial appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News carried the story twice, first on Dec. 27 among a 'batch of home Christmas tragedies' under the line 'Riot at Oconee—Fears of Further Trouble', and again on Dec. 28 as 'The Oconee Riot.' Both Savannah reports laid the trouble on the Black men, stressing that they were drinking, came armed and 'fired the first pistol', and they described the whites as fearing 'trouble from the negroes.' The second report's dateline read 'Dec. 15', although it told the same Monday fight and Tuesday call to Toomsboro as the first.

A Macon wire dated Dec. 30 carried the story out of the state, to the Washington Evening Critic as 'A Georgia Riot', to the St. Paul Daily Globe as 'Race Riot in Georgia', and to the New York Sun as 'A Marshal Attacked by Negroes.' The Sun's fuller text called the Washingtons 'a family of drunken negroes' and Lawson 'a negro desperado.'

The papers disagreed about Lawson: the Critic and the Globe reported 'Asa Lawson' killed, the Globe listing him among 'white men', while the Sun called 'Ira Lawson' a Black man who was seriously hurt but not killed. The Globe also called Webster and his son William 'mortally wounded', whereas the local Sandersville dispatch said the marshal was doing well. The Georgia dispatches, closer to the scene, reported no deaths, and the Sun's version, which explains Lawson's part, is the fullest text of the Macon wire.

reader.title: Oconee riot of 1882
bases: A town marshal's attempt to arrest Black men turned into a gun and knife fight in which the marshal, his son, the mayor and white citizens shot several Black men (A2, A3, A5).

A Sandersville dispatch (A2), a Toomsboro dispatch (A3) and a Macon wire (A4-A6) independently report a riot at Oconee in which the marshal was hurt and Black men were shot, though dates and casualties differ.

accounts.label: Sandersville dispatch
accounts.gist: Drunken Black men were 'troublesome' on Saturday and one was arrested; on Monday they came back armed, three were shot and the marshal was seriously injured, and whites asked Toomsboro for help.

accounts.label: Toomsboro dispatch
accounts.gist: The marshal tried to arrest fighting Black men and was resisted; Black men fired first, hitting the marshal's son, who mortally wounded one of them; a posse of ten came on Tuesday after rumors of a rescue.

accounts.label: Macon wire
accounts.gist: Versions differ: Asa Lawson killed and the Websters badly or mortally wounded (A4, A6), or a Christmas row in which five Washington brothers resisted arrest and Ira Lawson, Black, was the only one seriously hurt (A5).

framing.detail: Georgia dispatches blamed 'negroes' who were drunk, came 'armed' and 'fired the first pistol', and reported whites' fears of 'trouble from the negroes'.
Northern papers ran the Macon wire under 'A Georgia Riot', 'Race Riot in Georgia' and 'A Marshal Attacked by Negroes', with a 'negro desperado' and 'drunken negroes'.

versions.value: Monday under a Dec. 15 dateline, i.e. Dec. 11

conflicts.note: A3 tells the same sequence as A2 (Monday fight, Tuesday call to Toomsboro) and was printed the day after A2; its 'Dec. 15' dateline is probably a misprint. A5 ties the Macon wire to Christmas Day, so A4 and A6's timing likely reflects when the wire was sent.

versions.value: Ira Lawson, Black 'desperado', seriously hurt but not killed

conflicts.note: A5 is the fuller version of the same Macon wire and is the only one that explains Lawson's part.

info: Christmas Day, Monday, Dec. 25, 1882 (A2, A5); A3's 'Monday' under a 'Dec. 15' dateline would be Dec. 11; the Macon wire variously gives 'last night' or 'to-day' relative to Dec. 30
Black men wounded: three shot, one likely to die (A2); one 'mortally wounded' (A3); Handy, Jefferson and Squire Washington 'dangerously wounded' (A6); four wounded (A5)
